Yes—there is a paper by Khoat Than on fairness limits: No-Free-Fairness: Fundamental Limits and Trade-offs in Learning Systems [1]. It argues that learning systems face fundamental fairness limits from three sources: irreducible subgroup cost creates an inherent fairness–cost frontier, finite-sample learning alone can induce subgroup disparity even when a perfectly fair and accurate solution exists, and limited model expressivity can make fairness unattainable regardless of data or training procedure [1].

More specifically, the paper states that strict relative fairness can create a statistical bottleneck where achieving low cost may require exponentially many samples, and it rules out distribution-free fairness guarantees in finite-sample settings [1]. Related papers discuss practical fairness trade-offs rather than these impossibility limits, such as tolerating small false-negative-rate differences in criminal justice [2] or balancing fairness with hard resource constraints in threshold optimization [3].
